reasoning: 1. TARGET ENGAGEMENT: Strong evidence of target engagement - verubecestat significantly reduced cortical amyloid SUVR (-0.05 to -0.06 vs +0.02 placebo, p<0.0001), confirming BACE1 inhibition and reduced amyloid production. 2. PATHWAY MODULATION: Mixed pathway signals - amyloid reduction was achieved as intended, but CSF total tau increased 33-43% vs 10% placebo, suggesting potential downstream pathway disruption or compensatory mechanisms. Hippocampal volume loss was similar across arms, indicating no neuroprotective benefit. 3. CLINICAL TRANSLATION: Primary endpoint (CDR-SB) failed - both 12mg (p=0.6734) and 40mg (p=0.0141 but worsening vs placebo) arms showed no clinical benefit despite target engagement. The 40mg arm actually showed significantly worse cognitive decline than placebo. 4. POPULATION EFFECTS: No subgroup analyses reported. 5. CONFOUNDERS: No major trial design issues - adequate sample size (1454), appropriate duration (130 weeks), placebo-controlled design. The failure appears mechanistic rather than methodological.

failure_modes.evidence: Target was engaged (amyloid SUVR reduced significantly) and intended biology moved (amyloid production decreased), but clinical endpoint (CDR-SB) failed to improve and actually worsened in the 40mg arm vs placebo

edges_to_update.reasoning: Despite achieving the intended biology (amyloid reduction confirmed by SUVR), clinical outcomes worsened, strongly contradicting the hypothesis that amyloid reduction drives clinical benefit in prodromal AD
While amyloid SUVR decreased, the increase in CSF tau and lack of clinical benefit suggests the mechanism may have unintended downstream effects that offset the intended amyloid reduction
